title: Crack mitigating and microstructure engineering through in-process mechanical work in wire directed energy deposited Invar alloy
abstract: Abstract Wire-based directed energy deposition (WDED) of Invar alloys is prone to cracking due to high thermal stresses and microstructural anisotropy. In this study, in-process machine hammer peening (MHP) was integrated into WDED to mitigate cracking and control the microstructure of Invar alloy. The as-deposited material exhibited millimetre-scale columnar grains with strong build-directional alignment and severe solidification cracking along grain boundaries, indicating a dominant role of deposition-induced thermal stresses. Interlayer MHP promoted a transition from epitaxial growth to heterogeneous nucleation, producing a refined and more equiaxed grain structure with improved tolerance to thermal straining. Deformation-related FCC texture components and an increased fraction of low-energy Σ3 coincidence site lattice boundaries were observed in the MHP-treated material, contributing to enhanced grain-boundary-mediated plasticity and cracking resistance. Mechanical characterisation further revealed increased hardness and elastic modulus achieved by interlayer MHP, together with progressive build-height-dependent strengthening. In general, in-process MHP offers an effective and cost-efficient thermo-mechanical strategy for crack mitigation and is expected to contribute to microstructure-property optimisation in additively manufactured Invar alloys.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Invar alloy (namely FeNi36) is a single-phase face-centred cubic (FCC) alloy that exhibits exceptional dimensional stability up to its Curie temperature, arising from its unique magnetostrictive behaviour [ 1 ]. This property makes Invar a critical material for applications demanding stringent dimensional tolerances under thermal loading, including composite tooling for aircraft structures, precision optical mountings, metrology instruments, time-keeping devices, and seismic creep gauges [ 2 ]. Conventional manufacture of Invar components relies primarily on casting followed by extensive machining. However, the fully austenitic microstructure leads to severe tool wear, resulting in poor machinability, high material waste, and elevated production costs. These inherent limitations, combined with the high cost of raw material, make Invar particularly well suited to additive manufacturing (AM). In addition to the design freedom, material savings, reduced lead times and the potential to deposit functionally graded parts, is drawing researchers rapidly towards implementing AM technology for Invar parts [ 3 ,  4 ,  5 – 6 ].

Previous studies have demonstrated that the coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) and mechanical properties of Invar alloy manufactured by selective laser melting (SLM) is highly sensitive to processing parameters, particularly laser energy density and scanning strategy. Different optimal energy densities have been reported for island, rotated parallel, and meander scanning strategies, highlighting the strong influence of scanning-induced thermal history on cooling rate and microstructural evolution [ 7 ,  8 – 9 ]. Excessive energy input promotes keyhole formation, whereas insufficient energy leads to lack-of-fusion defects [ 10 ]. Mechanical anisotropy has also been observed, with significantly higher ductility in horizontally tested specimens compared to vertically tested ones, indicating interlayer lack-of-fusion defects aligned perpendicular to the build direction [ 11 ]. Although post-processing treatments such as hot isostatic pressing can reduce porosity, careful control of cooling rate is required to avoid residual stress accumulation and grain boundary cracking [ 11 ,  12 ]. Moreover, the complex thermal gradients inherent to SLM govern dendritic morphology, resulting in heterogeneous structures across neighboring grains [ 13 ]. While the effect of build density on the CTE has been reported [ 11 ,  14 ], the influence of dendritic morphology on CTE remains largely unexplored. In addition, laser melting of mechanically alloyed Fe–Ni powders has been shown to produce finer grains and grain-boundary precipitates compared with pre-alloyed powders, likely due to sluggish solid-state diffusion and non-equilibrium phase evolution in the Fe–Ni system [ 15 ,  16 ]. Although powder-based AM processes such as SLM offer high dimensional accuracy, wire-based directed energy deposition (WDED) has attracted increasing research attention due to its capability to manufacture large-scale components with high deposition rate while maintaining near-net-shape geometries [ 17 ]. However, WDED processes are typically associated with high heat input and multiple reheating cycles. Sood et al. [ 18 ] reported that Invar deposited by WDED (gas tungsten arc) exhibits coarse columnar austenitic grains, resulting in pronounced anisotropy in both mechanical properties and CTE. The grain size increased with increased heat input, promoting cracking along grain boundaries due to continuous thermal straining and ductility exhaustion during successive layer depositions. Another study [ 19 ] focusing on WDED (cold metal transfer) processed FeNi36 reported that the cracking susceptibility of this alloy is greatly reduced by the addition of 1.58 wt% Nb and 0.22 wt% C as alloying elements which form precipitated phases of (Nb, Ti)C in the γ grains. These precipitates have been reported to enhance the tensile property of the alloy, with simultaneous reduction in cracking susceptibility [ 19 ].

The inherently low tensile strength and hardness of Invar have also motivated extensive research efforts. Previous studies have demonstrated that the addition of microalloying elements such as V, Ti, Nb, Cr, W, Mo, and Zr can enhance mechanical properties through grain refinement and precipitation strengthening mechanisms [ 20 ,  21 ]. However, certain alloying additions, including Nb and Zr, significantly increase material cost [ 21 ], while others such as Mo and Cr have been shown to degrade high-temperature thermal stability, which is governed by magnetic interactions among Ni–Ni, Fe–Ni, and Fe–Fe atomic pairs [ 22 ,  23 ]. Alternatively, strength enhancement in as-cast Invar has been achieved through strain hardening and grain refinement via cold rolling, owing to the presence of multiple active slip systems in the FCC austenitic phase that readily accommodate severe plastic deformation [ 20 ]. These findings suggest that, for Invar alloys, the most effective strategy to improve mechanical properties without compromising high-temperature thermal stability is through grain refinement combined with increased dislocation density induced by deformation-based microstructural refinement [ 20 ,  24 ].

In-process mechanical work, including rolling and peening, has been shown to be an effective strategy for microstructure control in WDED process [ 25 ,  26 ]. Such approaches disrupt the formation of coarse columnar grains and strong textures, promoting grain refinement and improved microstructural isotropy [ 27 ,  28 ]. Also, deformation-induced stored strain drives recrystallisation during subsequent thermal cycles, with the refinement efficiency further influenced by alloy chemistry and reheating behaviour [ 29 ,  30 ]. In this work, in-process machine hammer peening (MHP) was applied during the WDED process of Invar and corresponding influence in grain refinement and crack mitigation was evaluated. This work demonstrates that interlayer MHP can effectively mitigate solidification cracking and refine the solidification microstructure in WDED Invar, providing new insights into the application of thermomechanical treatments for crack-sensitive alloys in additive manufacturing.

sections.heading: Manufacturing process
paragraphs: The experimental set-up consisted of a EWM T552 Tetrix plasma power source with a wire feeder, a local shielding device to protect the melt pool from oxidation, a 6-axis Kuka robot for mounting the plasma torch for deposition and a pneumatic MHP tool for interlayer peening. The welding process was monitored using a Xiris ®  welding camera. The deposition was carried using a 1.2 mm diameter wire and on a 12.7 mm thick hot-rolled Invar substrate. Chemical composition for the substrate and wire is shown in Table  1 .

A single pass deposition strategy, where the torch moves in a linear path, and torch travel direction changes by 180 degrees between each layer, was used to build two single-pass walls, (a) as-deposited condition – 200 mm (length) by 22 mm (height) by 10 mm (thickness), and (b) MHP condition – 200 mm (length) by 12 mm (height) by 12 mm (thickness) size. For MHP condition, MHP was applied to each layer using a single straight-track traversed approximately along the walls centre line. The schematic of the experimental set-up is shown in Fig.  1 . The key parameters used for WDED deposition and successive in-process MHP processes are presented in Table  2 . The parameters used for both WDED and MHP were selected based on preliminary trials to ensure stable deposition, consistent bead geometry, and effective mechanical treatment without causing excessive deformation or surface damage. Also, due to the extremely low coefficient of thermal expansion of Invar alloys, the influence of the determined interlayer temperature on thermal stress accumulation is expected to be limited.

The reference frame employed throughout is: building direction—ND, torch/tool travel direction—TD, and thickness of the wall referred to normal direction—ND

sections.heading: Material characterisation
paragraphs: Two different cross-sectional areas were studied for optical macroscopic and microstructure observations using Zeiss Stemi 508 stereo microscope, area bound by building direction (BD) and (a) torch/tool travel direction (TD) and (b) thickness of the wall referred to normal direction (ND). Samples for metallographic examinations were prepared according to ASTM E3 standard [ 31 ] and etched using Aqua Regia (1:3 molar ratio of HNO 3  and HCl) solution for 20 s to reveal the microstructure. Electron back scatter diffraction (EBSD) scanning was carried out using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FEGSEM, TESCAN S8000G) equipped with a high-speed Oxford Symmetry ®  S3 EBSD detector to compare the microstructure and crystallographic orientation in different conditions. The EBSD settings include current of 15 nA, voltage of 20 keV, step size of 2 μm, and scan size of at least 1 mm by 2.5 mm across two more layers to quantitatively observe and analyse grain and sub-structures formed in the deposits under the different processing conditions. The indexing rate of all EBSD maps conducted is above 95%, showing good quality data. Crystallographic related analyses were performed using Aztec Crystal 3.1 software. Microhardness measurements were taken along the BD of the sample using an Innovatest Falcon 503 micro-Vickers hardness testing machine, applying a 200 g load for 10 s. Indentations started from 0.5 mm from the top and were spaced 0.5 mm apart. Nanoindentation measurement was performed using an Ultra Nanoindentation Tester, CSM Instruments SA now Anton Paar ®  on as-deposited condition, MHP condition, and Invar substrate material which represents the standard properties for conventionally hot rolled condition. A 100 mN load was applied in the sequence with 10 by 10 array of measurement points and a step size of 50 μm (to avoid possible interference between indentations), resulting in a mapped area of 500 μm by 500 μm.

sections.heading: Macro morphologies and microstructure comparison
paragraphs: The macro and optical micrographs of the as-deposited Invar single-pass wall were shown in Fig.  2 . At the macroscopic scale, surface and through-thickness cracks are clearly visible in different sectioning planes (Fig.  2 a–c).

In the BD–ND plane, cracks are observed to propagate predominantly 10°–15° to the BD of the wall, which also coincides with the direction of grain epitaxial growth. In the BD–TD plane, multiple vertical macroscopic cracks extend across several deposited layers and are visible across the entire wall., suggesting a strong correlation between crack propagation and the thermal gradient during deposition. These cracks appear to be approximately equidistant, indicating that the ductility of the deposited wall has been exhausted and it can no longer accommodate the longitudinal thermal stresses generated by the repeated rapid heating and cooling cycles during successive layer deposition [ 32 ]. Although build height can influence the accumulation of residual stresses, it is worth noting that cracking initiates during the solidification of the early deposited layers and subsequently propagates along BD as additional layers are added.

Such cracking behaviour is characteristic of solidification-related cracking commonly reported in fusion-based processing of Invar alloys. The coarse columnar grains formed during directional solidification reduce the ability of the material to accommodate solidification shrinkage and thermal stresses, thereby promoting intergranular crack initiation along the grain boundaries. In addition, the repeated reheating cycles associated with the layer-by-layer deposition process may further promote crack propagation along these weakened grain boundaries. At higher magnification (Fig.  2 d, e), variations in dendritic sub-grain morphology are observed, with some grains exhibiting regular cellular dendrites, while others display fine elongated dendritic structures. However, these differences in sub-grain morphology do not appear to be the primary cause of reheating crack formation, as grains with similar dendritic morphologies also exhibit cracking, as indicated by the red arrows.

Overall, cracking in WDED-fabricated Invar is controlled by the combined effects of high heat input, steep thermal gradients, and repeated reheating cycles. These conditions promote columnar grain growth, segregation band formation, and the accumulation of thermal strain. The strong alignment of cracks with BD and dendritic morphology highlights the critical role of thermal–microstructural anisotropy in governing crack susceptibility in additively manufactured Invar alloys. The high heat input and associated thermal stresses in WDED processes are well documented [ 11 ,  33 ], and pose a significant challenge when processing alloys susceptible to solidification cracking. In addition, coarse columnar grains may promote local compositional heterogeneity through dendritic segregation. Such compositional variations may result in local differences in thermal expansion behaviour and could contribute to crack initiation and propagation. However, this hypothesis was not directly verified in the present study [ 15 ]. Furthermore, the columnar alignment of grain boundaries causes the maximum longitudinal thermal stresses to act predominantly in opening mode for any dislocation clusters formed at these weak interfaces, thereby facilitating crack initiation and propagation [ 3 ]. In addition to the microstructural anisotropy, chemical heterogeneity arising from solute segregation during solidification may further contribute to crack initiation in the as-deposited condition [ 34 ]. Under the high heat input and directional solidification conditions of WDED, redistribution of Fe and Ni occurs at the dendritic scale, leading to local compositional variations. These variations can result in differences in thermal expansion behaviour and local mechanical response between neighbouring regions, thereby promoting strain localisation and facilitating crack initiation along grain boundaries. Furthermore, tensile residual stresses are likely to develop during the WDED process due to the steep thermal gradients and repeated thermal cycling typically associated with this process, as reported in previous studies. These stresses are predominantly aligned along the build direction and act in opening mode on columnar grain boundaries, which are already weakened by segregation and solidification cracking behaviour. Therefore, chemical heterogeneity together with the possible presence of tensile residual stresses may contribute to crack initiation and propagation in the as-deposited material.

Fig. 2 Macro morphology of the as-deposited Invar single-pass wall showing the crack features in different planes and scales;  a  macro morphology taken from BD-ND plane,  b ,  c  macrostructures in BD-TD plane, detailed view of the reheat cracks in  d  BD–ND plane and  e  BD–TD plane

After applying interlayer MHP during deposition process, significant changes can be found in both the macro morphology and microstructure, as shown in Fig.  3 . The overall appearance of the Invar single-pass wall with interlayer MHP treatment is presented in Fig.  3 a, where the MHP-treated surface region is highlighted by the dotted blue line. The wall exhibits a uniform geometry along the deposition length, with no visible surface cracking following the application of interlayer MHP. Figure  3 b presents a macrograph of the wall sectioned in the BD–TD plane, revealing a continuous and defect-free morphology throughout the build height. The absence of macroscopic cracks in the MHP-treated wall contrasts markedly with the crack-prone as-deposited condition, demonstrating the effectiveness of MHP in suppressing reheating-induced cracking during WDED. Higher-magnification microstructural observations of the MHP-affected region (Fig.  3 c) reveal a refined and more equiaxed grain structure compared with the coarse columnar and dendritic morphologies typically observed in as-deposited Invar. The refined grains exhibit disrupted dendritic substructures and reduced alignment with the build direction, suggesting that the repeated plastic deformation introduced by MHP promotes grain subdivision and recrystallisation during subsequent thermal cycles. Notably, the grain morphology of the MHP-treated Invar (Fig.  3 c) is comparable to that of the hot-rolled alloy (Fig.  3 d), i.e., the substrate. Although repeated reheating cycles continue to reduce the intrinsic ductility of the alloy, the introduction of plastic strain through MHP promotes the formation of multiple heterogeneous nucleation sites rather than epitaxial grain growth. This results in a more randomly oriented grain structure with a significantly increased grain boundary area, which enhances matrix plasticity and improves the ability of the material to accommodate large thermal strains without crack formation. The formation of fine, equiaxed grains effectively suppresses the alignment of weak columnar γ grain boundaries along the build direction, thereby orienting these interfaces orthogonally to the direction of maximum thermal tensile stress, which reduces crack initiation and propagation [ 35 ].

Fig. 3 a  Macro morphology of the Invar single-pass wall deposited by WDED with the interlayer MHP surface highlighted by the dotted blue line,  b  macro image showing macro morphology in BD-TD plane,  c  microstructure in the MHP-affected region,  d  microstructure of the hot-rolled FeNi36 substrate for comparison

sections.heading: Analysis of grain boundary, orientation and texture
paragraphs: EBSD characterisation in as-deposited and in-process MHP condition were carried out to objectively compare the grain boundary, size orientation and texture with conventionally processed (i.e., hot rolled annealed) Invar alloy. The as-deposited WDED Invar (Fig.  4 a1) exhibits coarse, elongated columnar γ grains with a small number of {100} family of crystal oriented along the deposition direction, indicating no preferred grain orientation in the build direction which is different from the strong <001> texture reported for SLM Invar [ 10 ]. However, it should be noted that the number of grains in the mapped area is limited due to the large grain size in the order of a few millimetres. The corresponding grain boundary map (Fig.  4 a2) reveals a microstructure dominated by high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs), with a negligible fraction of special coincidence site lattice (CSL) boundaries (Σ3 and Σ9), highlighting the highly anisotropic and crack-susceptible nature of the as-deposited microstructure. As-deposited WDED Invar also exhibited ductility dip cracking at the grain boundaries shown in Fig.  5 a1 in the missing indexes areas shown by the row of arrows. However, the size scales of these reheat cracks were much larger than those reported in SLM-deposited Invar [ 13 ]. The significantly higher heat input and consequently the wider heat affected zone which resulted in epitaxial grain growth in WAAM FeNi36 is responsible for this behaviour.

In contrast, the MHP-treated WDED Invar shows a markedly refined and equiaxed grain structure (Fig.  4 b1), with a more heterogeneous and less directionally aligned crystallographic orientation compared with the as-deposited condition. The grain size distribution was primarily fine (< 40 μm), but with few spots of relatively coarse grains (~ 160 μm). From Fig.  4 b1 and b2, it can be inferred that the common feature between these interspersed coarse grains in the MHP Invar was the type of grain boundary, i.e., HAGB and the orientation direction as <001> and <111>. This can happen due to preferential growth of few grains suitably oriented to consume neighbouring grains and grow [ 36 ]. However, the overall grain structure map shows that the grains are randomly oriented. The grain boundary map (Fig.  4 b2) also reveals a pronounced increase in grain boundary density and a clear enhancement in the fraction of CSL boundaries, which is commonly associated with recrystallisation-related twin formation during thermal cycling. For comparison, the hot-rolled Invar substrate (Fig.  4 c1) exhibits a homogeneous equiaxed grain structure with random crystallographic orientations, characteristic of a fully recrystallised microstructure processed under thermomechanical equilibrium conditions. The corresponding grain boundary network (Fig.  4 c2) shows the highest density of CSL boundaries among all conditions, serving as a benchmark microstructure with superior ductility and damage tolerance.

Quantitative grain size analysis (Fig.  4 d) further confirms the substantial grain refinement induced by MHP. The as-deposited condition exhibits a broad grain size distribution with equivalent circle diameters extending to the millimetre scale (actual value could be even larger owing to the epitaxial grain morphology spanning over several layers and exceeding the mapped area), whereas the MHP-treated Invar shows a pronounced shift toward smaller grain sizes, approaching the distribution observed in the hot-rolled substrate. The increased population of fine grains reflects the effective interruption of epitaxial grain growth and the activation of heterogeneous nucleation sites through deformation-induced stored energy. In addition, Fig.  4 e compares the area fraction of CSL (Σ3 and Σ9) across different conditions. The as-deposited Invar contains a negligible fraction of CSL boundaries, while MHP treatment increases the Σ3 boundary fraction from ~ 0.9% (as-deposited) to ~ 21.3%, although it remains well below the hot-rolled substrate (~ 63.1%). Since Σ3 and related CSL boundaries are known to possess lower boundary energy and enhanced resistance to crack initiation and propagation, but introduction of such grain boundaries frequently requires thermomechanical processing routes [ 37 ]. Formation of CSL, in particular Σ3, is significant as it provides the additional plasticity required by matrix to withstand the additional thermal strain by a previously deposited layer from the successive layers. This would be very beneficial for applications requiring better mechanical properties and can be implemented with much lower facility cost as compared to setting up thermomechanical processing facilities.

Fig. 4 Inverse pole figure (IPF) maps and corresponding grain boundary maps in different conditions:  a1 ,  a2  as-deposited WDED Invar,  b1 ,  b2  MHP-treated WDED Invar,  c1  hot rolled Invar substrate; Comparison of  d  FCC equivalent circle diameter distribution and  e  area fraction of special grain boundaries (Σ3, Σ9) for as-deposited, MHP and substrate conditions. The crystal orientation-color relation map corresponding to the color-coded stereographic triangle inverse pole figure (IPF) is inserted in the top-right corner of Fig. 4a1
Fig. 5 a1 ,  a2  Grain orientation spread (GOS) map and distribution and ( b1 ,  b2 ) Kernel average misorientation (KAM) map and distribution for MHP-treated Invar

The grain orientation spread (GOS) and kernel average misorientation (KAM) maps of the MHP-treated sample provide further insight into the deformation state of the microstructure, as shown in Fig.  5 . The relatively high GOS values and the broad distribution centred between 3° and 9° indicate significant intragranular lattice distortion, while the KAM distribution reveals pronounced local misorientation associated with a high density of geometrically necessary dislocations. These results confirm that interlayer MHP introduces substantial plastic deformation and dislocation accumulation within the deposited layers. The deformation-induced substructures therefore provide the stored strain energy required for grain subdivision and facilitate recovery and recrystallisation during the subsequent reheating cycles associated with layer-by-layer deposition. As a result, the combined effect of plastic deformation and repeated thermal cycles leads to the observed grain refinement and increased fraction of special grain boundaries in the MHP-treated WDED Invar. This transformation from epitaxial columnar growth to a deformation-assisted recrystallisation mechanism is also consistent with the suppression of crack formation observed at the macroscopic scale.

Figure  6  presents the orientation distribution functions (ODFs) of the FCC-γ phase at φ 2  = 0°, 45°, and 60° for the different processing conditions. The as-deposited WDED Invar (Fig.  6 a) exhibits pronounced texture components with high orientation density concentrated at discrete locations in Euler space, with an texture index of 4.71 and maximum orientation density reaches approximately 20.1 m.r.d., indicative of strong preferential crystallographic alignment induced by directional solidification and epitaxial grain growth under steep thermal gradients. Following interlayer MHP, a substantial redistribution of orientation density is observed in the ODFs (Fig.  6 b). Although distinct texture components remain, their peak intensities are significantly reduced, with the texture index reducing significantly to 1.54 and the maximum orientation density decreasing to approximately 4.6 m.r.d. Compared with the as-deposited condition, the MHP-treated Invar exhibits a more diffuse distribution of orientations, indicating a breakdown of the sharp deposition-induced texture and a transition toward a deformation-influenced texture state. Notably, the MHP-treated Invar shows the emergence and strengthening of specific FCC deformation-related texture components, particularly the {110}⟨110⟩ R-Goss ND  and {110}⟨111⟩ Goss/Brass orientations. These components are characteristic of FCC alloys subjected to plane-strain deformation and shear and are commonly associated with deformation-induced lattice rotation and slip activity rather than epitaxial growth [ 38 ]. The development of R-Goss ND  and Goss/Brass components indicates that the introduction of plastic strain via MHP alters the dominant texture formation mechanism from thermally driven directional solidification to deformation-controlled crystallographic rotation and grain subdivision. This texture transition is consistent with the observed refinement and loss of columnar grain alignment, as well as the increased grain boundary density reported in Fig.  5 . In contrast, the hot-rolled Invar substrate (Fig.  6 c) exhibits a nearly random texture (texture index ≈ 1.02) with a dominant {001}⟨100⟩ Cube texture, which is characteristic of a fully recrystallised FCC alloy following thermomechanical processing [ 39 ]. The presence of a strong Cube component and the absence of sharp deformation-related texture features indicate that the substrate has reached a near-equilibrium recrystallised state. Overall, the ODF analysis demonstrates that interlayer MHP fundamentally modifies the texture evolution of WDED Invar by reducing the dominance of deposition-induced crystallographic alignment and promoting deformation-related texture components. Although the MHP-treated material does not reach the fully recrystallised Cube texture state of the hot-rolled substrate, the substantial reduction in texture sharpness and the emergence of deformation-controlled orientations provide a mechanistic basis for the improved isotropy and enhanced resistance to reheating-induced cracking observed in the MHP-treated builds.

Fig. 6 Orientation distribution functions (ODFs) with φ 2  = 0°, 45°, and 60° of the texture components of FCC-γ phase in different conditions:  a  as-deposited WDED Invar,  b  MHP-treated WDED Invar,  c  hot rolled Invar substrate

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs: The mechanical property evolution of WDED Invar under different processing conditions are compared in Fig.  7 , as characterised by nano-indentation and Vickers micro-hardness measurements. Figure  7 a shows the averaged nano-indentation load–displacement curves for the as-deposited, MHP-treated, and hot-rolled substrate materials. The as-deposited Invar exhibits a larger penetration depth at a given load, indicating a lower resistance to plastic deformation. In contrast, the MHP-treated material shows a steeper loading slope and a reduced maximum penetration depth, reflecting a deformation-strengthened response induced by interlayer mechanical work. The hot-rolled substrate exhibits a load–displacement response intermediate between the as-deposited and MHP-treated conditions, consistent with a recrystallised microstructure with lower stored deformation energy than the MHP-treated material but higher resistance to plastic deformation than the as-deposited condition.

The elastic modulus and hardness values extracted from nano-indentation data are compared in Fig.  7 b. The as-deposited condition exhibits the lowest elastic modulus and hardness, whereas the MHP-treated material shows the highest values for both properties. The increase in hardness can be directly attributed to deformation-induced strengthening arising from grain refinement and the accumulation of dislocations introduced by repeated interlayer hammer peening. The elevated elastic modulus observed in the MHP-treated material can be associated with a combination of factors, including increased constraint on elastic deformation due to the high dislocation density, refined grain structure, and the presence of deformation-induced texture components, as revealed by the EBSD and ODF analyses. In addition, residual compressive stresses introduced by interlayer mechanical work may also contribute to the apparent increase in indentation modulus [ 40 ]. Figure  7 c further compares the Vickers micro-hardness distribution along BD for the as-deposited and MHP-treated walls. The as-deposited condition exhibits relatively low and uniform hardness values, indicating limited work hardening despite repeated thermal cycling. In contrast, the MHP-treated wall shows a clear and progressive increase in hardness with distance from the substrate, reaching values significantly higher than those of the as-deposited material. The hardness gradient observed along the build height is likely associated with the combined effects of interlayer plastic deformation and subsequent thermal cycling. The lower regions of the build experience a greater number of reheating cycles during deposition, which may promote recovery and partial recrystallization, thereby reducing the stored strain energy and dislocation density. In contrast, the upper regions experience fewer reheating cycles and therefore retain a higher degree of deformation-induced strengthening, resulting in higher hardness values [ 41 ].

In summary, the mechanical characterisation demonstrates that interlayer MHP effectively transforms the mechanical response of WDED Invar from a soft, crack-prone state to a strengthened and more damage-tolerant condition. The observed improvements in hardness and elastic modulus correlate directly with the microstructural refinement, increased fraction of deformation-related textures, and enhanced grain boundary density induced by MHP. These results provide a clear mechanistic link between in-process mechanical work, microstructure engineering, and the mitigation of reheating-induced cracking in additively manufactured Invar alloys.

Fig. 7 a  Nano indentation load versus displacement curves (averaged) for as-deposited, MHP and substrate material refers to the conventionally processed FeNi36 in hot rolled, annealed conditions,  b  comparison of elastic modulus and hardness values for the three conditions obtained from nano-indentation,  c  Vicker micro-hardness transition comparison of as-deposited and MHP conditions

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: In this investigation, in-process MHP is applied to the WDED process of manufacturing Invar alloy to mitigate inherent crack issues. Microstructure and mechanical properties in as-deposited and MHP-treated conditions were systematically compared with that of the conventionally processed (hot rolled, annealed) Invar substrate. The main findings can be summarised as:

As-deposited WDED Invar exhibits large ‘mm’ sized columnar grains with strong orientation along building direction and suffers from solidification cracking at the grain boundaries. All the reheat cracks were oriented in the build direction, which indicates that the driving force for these cracks arises from the thermal stresses generated in the deposition direction, during the deposition of successive layers. The application of interlayer MHP in the WDED process enhances the ability of Invar to withstand process-induced thermal straining, promoting a transition in the grain refinement mechanism from epitaxial growth to heterogeneous nucleation, leading to the formation of generally finer equiaxed microstructure. MHP-treated Invar shows the emergence and strengthening of specific FCC deformation-related texture components, particularly the {110}⟨110⟩ R-GossND and {110}⟨111⟩ Goss/Brass orientations, indicates that the introduction of plastic strain via MHP alters the dominant texture formation mechanism from thermally driven directional solidification to deformation-controlled crystallographic rotation. Interlayer MHP was shown to substantially increase the fraction of low-energy Σ3 CSL boundaries in WDED Invar, thereby enhancing grain-boundary-mediated plasticity and resistance to thermal strain–induced cracking, while providing a cost-effective alternative to conventional thermomechanical processing routes. Interlayer MHP significantly enhances the mechanical response of WDED Invar, leading to markedly increased hardness and elastic modulus and a progressive build-height-dependent strengthening behaviour, in contrast to the softer as-deposited state and the recrystallised hot-rolled substrate.
